title: Turing Machines & Computability
summary: The Turing machine model, decidability, and the halting problem — the line between what's computable at all and what isn't.

slides.subTitle: Tape, head, states
slides.markdown:
A **Turing machine** is a finite set of states plus an unbounded **tape** and a **head** that reads/writes one cell at a time and can move left or right. Each step: read the symbol under the head, write a symbol, move, and change state.

![The Turing machine model: tape, head, and finite control](assets/turing-machine-model.svg)

That's the whole model. No stack, no special structures — just unbounded tape and simple per-step rules.

slides.subTitle: The Church-Turing thesis
slides.markdown:
The **Church-Turing thesis** claims: anything intuitively "computable" (by any reasonable notion of algorithm) is computable by a Turing machine. It isn't a provable theorem — it's a claim about the informal notion of "algorithm" matching a precise mathematical model.

Every serious alternative model tried (lambda calculus, RAM machines, real programming languages) has been proven **equally powerful** to a Turing machine — this convergence is the strongest evidence for the thesis.

Practically: "is this computable" and "can a Turing machine do it" are treated as the same question.

slides.subTitle: Decidable vs undecidable
slides.markdown:
A problem is **decidable** if some Turing machine always halts and correctly answers yes/no for every input. It's **undecidable** if no such machine exists — not "hard," but *provably impossible*, no matter how much cleverness you throw at it.

This is stronger than "NP-hard" — NP-hard problems are still solvable, just slowly. Undecidable problems have **no algorithm at all**, ever.

Most problems you'll meet are decidable; undecidability is reserved for a specific class involving self-reference or search over programs themselves.

slides.subTitle: The statement
slides.markdown:
The **halting problem**: given a program `P` and input `x`, decide whether `P` halts on `x` or runs forever.

This sounds like a normal (if hard) engineering problem — but Turing proved in 1936 that **no algorithm can solve it correctly for every possible program and input**. It's the single most-cited result in computability theory, and the template every other undecidability proof reduces to.

It's not about a specific tricky program — it's a statement that *no general-purpose halting-checker* can exist, period.

slides.subTitle: The diagonalization argument
slides.markdown:
Assume a halting-checker `H(P, x)` exists. Build a new program `D(P)` that: runs `H(P, P)`, then does the **opposite** — loops forever if `H` says "halts," halts if `H` says "loops forever."

Now ask: does `D(D)` halt? If `H` says yes (halts), `D` is built to loop forever instead — contradiction. If `H` says no (loops), `D` halts instead — also a contradiction. Either way, `H` was wrong.

So no correct `H` can exist. This self-referential trick — feeding a machine its own description — is the same core idea as Cantor's diagonal argument and Russell's paradox.

slides.subTitle: Reductions
slides.markdown:
To prove a *new* problem `X` undecidable, you don't repeat diagonalization — you show solving `X` would let you solve the halting problem, via a **reduction**: if a hypothetical solver for `X` existed, you could build a halting-checker from it.

Since the halting problem has no solver, `X` can't either. Standard recipe: assume `X` decidable, use it to decide halting, contradiction, conclude `X` undecidable.

Questions like "does this program ever print `hello`" or "are these two programs equivalent" are proven undecidable exactly this way.

This is why no static-analysis tool can perfectly detect infinite loops or fully-general dead code: "does this loop terminate" and "is this path reachable" both reduce to the halting problem for some inputs.

Real tools don't try to solve the impossible general case — they use **conservative approximations**: flag likely-infinite loops heuristically, accept some false positives/negatives, and say "can't determine" rather than claim unbacked certainty.

This is a deliberate, correct design choice — not a gap a smarter tool could fix.

slides.subTitle: Undecidable in general ≠ unsolvable in every case
slides.markdown:
"The halting problem is undecidable" means **no single algorithm works for every possible program**. It does **not** mean you can't determine whether *your specific* loop halts.

Most real loops are trivially analyzable — bounded counters, simple recursion with a clear base case. Termination checkers solve the halting question correctly for large, useful subsets of real programs; they just can't be complete for *all* programs at once.

Don't over-generalize impossibility into "analysis is hopeless" — it's specifically the *every-program* version that's impossible.

slides.subTitle: Reducing a new problem to the halting problem
slides.markdown:
Prove: **"does program P ever print 'hello'"** is undecidable. Assume a solver `PrintsHello(P)` exists; build a halting-checker from it:

```
HaltChecker(P, x):
  Q = a new program that:
        runs P(x)
        then prints "hello"
  return PrintsHello(Q)
```

`Q` prints "hello" **if and only if** `P(x)` eventually finishes and control reaches the print statement — so `PrintsHello(Q)` correctly answers "does `P` halt on `x`." That's a full halting-checker, built entirely from the assumed `PrintsHello` solver. Since no halting-checker can exist, `PrintsHello` can't exist either — the same reduction template from the previous Card, applied concretely.
